Aim and objectives

Aim. To explain how randomised controlled trials are designed and protected from bias, and to calculate relative treatment effects from them.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Compare parallel, crossover, factorial and non-inferiority trial designs and identify when each is appropriate.
  2. Distinguish randomisation from allocation concealment and explain which bias each prevents.
  3. Explain how blinding prevents performance and detection bias, and distinguish single, double and triple blinding.
  4. Compare intention-to-treat and per-protocol analysis and describe ways of handling missing data, such as last observation carried forward.
  5. Calculate relative risk and relative risk reduction from trial data and interpret their 95% confidence intervals.
  6. Complete all 30 worked challenges, scoring at least 24 (80%), before you open the working.
  7. Answer every quick-recall card out loud, getting at least 80% right, by the end of today's session.

Part 1 · Core ideas

Category 113.3 · Experimental studies and trials

13.3.1Trial designs: who gets what, and when

Big idea. Every design is a different way of building a fair comparison, and each one buys fairness or efficiency at a stated price.
Picture it as a cafe trying a new recipe on its regulars.

Syllabus: Controlled and uncontrolled trials, n of 1 trials and other experimental designs: single-subject, pilot, adaptive, factorial, cluster randomised and crossover

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 104 · Crossover, cluster and factorial trials →

The story in plain words. Every trial asks the same question: did the treatment cause the change, or would it have happened anyway? A controlled trial answers by watching a comparison group at the same time. An uncontrolled before-and-after study measures one group twice and cannot separate the treatment from time or regression to the mean. A historical control borrows its comparison from the past: last year's patients on the old care against this year's on the new. When clinicians choose who gets which drug, the design is quasi-experimental and sicker patients drift towards one arm. That is confounding by indication, and a sample of thousands does not cure it. Within randomised trials the shape varies. Parallel groups each get one treatment. In a crossover everyone gets both in random order with a washout between. A factorial 2 x 2 trial tests two treatments at once in 4 groups. A cluster trial randomises wards or practices, and the sample is inflated by the design effect 1 + (m - 1) x ICC. ((? A ward trial recruits 21 patients per ward and the ICC is 0.05; what is the design effect? ?)) 1 + 20 x 0.05 = 2.0, so 300 individuals becomes 600.

The people and the evidence. Sacks, Chalmers and Smith (1982) compared trials of the same therapies built in two ways. Of 56 historically controlled trials, 44 found the new treatment better; of 50 randomised trials, only 10 did. Guyatt and colleagues (1986) brought the n of 1 trial to the bedside: one patient, repeated randomised and blinded pairs of active and placebo periods. It suits chronic, stable conditions and drugs that work and wear off quickly, and the answer belongs to that patient alone. Pallmann and colleagues (2018) set out how adaptive and platform trials drop arms or re-estimate sample size by rules written in advance.

From everyday life to the clinic. Picture a cafe testing a new recipe. Serving it this month and comparing with last month's reviews is a historical control. Giving each regular both dishes on different days, with a gap to clear the palate, is a crossover. Letting whole branches switch menus is a cluster trial, because one kitchen cannot cook two menus without mixing them. A pilot study checks whether families can be recruited and kept before anyone pays for the main trial; it is not powered for efficacy. An ABAB single-subject design counts one boy's head-banging through baseline, intervention, withdrawal and reinstatement. If it falls each time the support starts, the effect is convincing.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The commonest trap is calling an earlier cohort versus a later cohort a before-and-after study. Before-and-after means the same people measured twice. Different intakes in different years are historical controls. With a linked figure, read the legend before the bars. Crossover fails for treatments with lasting effects, such as psychotherapy, and for first episodes that may remit on their own. Factorial means two questions in four groups. Pilot means feasibility, not efficacy. Alternation, however tidy, is not randomisation, so allocation by order of referral makes a non-randomised controlled trial.

Sources
  1. Schulz KF, Chalmers I, Hayes RJ, Altman DG (1995). Empirical evidence of bias: dimensions of methodological quality associated with estimates of treatment effects in controlled trials. JAMA, 273: 408-412.
  2. Sibbald B, Roberts C (1998). Understanding controlled trials: crossover trials. BMJ, 316: 1719.
  3. Celentano DD, Szklo M (2019). Gordis Epidemiology, 6th ed. Elsevier.
  4. Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.
  5. Rothwell PM (2005). External validity of randomised controlled trials: "to whom do the results of this trial apply?" Lancet, 365: 82-93.
  6. Fleming TR, DeMets DL (1996). Surrogate end points in clinical trials: are we being misled? Ann Intern Med, 125: 605-613.
  7. Loudon K, Treweek S, Sullivan F et al. (2015). The PRECIS-2 tool: designing trials that are fit for purpose. BMJ, 350: h2147.

13.3.1.4Randomisation and allocation concealment

Big idea. Randomisation makes the groups comparable, and concealment stops anyone quietly undoing it at the door.
Picture it as a raffle drawn in another room.

Syllabus: Randomisation techniques such as simple, block, stratified, minimisation, cluster, adoptive

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 87 · RCTs: randomisation and blinding →

The story in plain words. Randomisation hands the choice of treatment to chance. Chance has no favourites, so on average it spreads age, severity, insight and everything nobody measured evenly between the arms. That is why a randomised difference can be read as cause. Simple randomisation is a coin toss or a computer list. It is fair, but in a small trial the arms can drift apart, as the figure shows. Block randomisation fixes this: in blocks of 4, every block holds two As and two Bs, so the arms never differ by more than two. ((? In the figure, why does the block line never pass +2? ?)) Each block of four must close level, so one arm can lead by at most two before the block finishes. Stratified randomisation runs a separate blocked list for each combination of key factors, such as sex by severity. Minimisation goes further: each new patient goes to whichever arm would best reduce imbalance among those already allocated, which suits small trials with many factors. Alternation, odd or even birth dates and record numbers are quasi-random: predictable, and therefore not randomisation.

The people and the evidence. In 1948 the Medical Research Council streptomycin trial, designed with Austin Bradford Hill, allocated patients from random sequences held in sealed envelopes at a central office. Clinicians could neither know nor choose the next allocation. That second idea is allocation concealment. Schulz and colleagues (1995) examined 250 trials from 33 meta-analyses. Trials with inadequate concealment reported odds ratios exaggerated by about 41%, and those with unclear concealment by about 30%. A random list is not enough; it has to be hidden.

From everyday life to the clinic. Imagine a raffle where the ticket seller can see the next prize. A friend might get the good one. Concealment means the draw happens in another room, after the ticket is sold. A central telephone or web service run by a third party is the gold standard; sealed, opaque, numbered envelopes are weaker because they can be opened or held to the light. On a recruiting ward, a psychiatrist who knows the next allocation is placebo may decide a very unwell patient is not quite suitable today. Nobody lied, yet the arms are no longer comparable. That is selection bias. Concealment is always possible, even in a psychotherapy trial where blinding is not.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Concealment works up to the moment of allocation; blinding works after it. If the stem says the recruiter telephones a trials unit after consent to learn the arm, the answer is concealment. Randomisation balances on average, not in every trial: a small trial can be unbalanced by chance, which is why the baseline table matters. Stratification factors are balanced by design, not left purely to chance. A coin toss is crude but random; alternation is tidy but not.

Sources
  1. Altman DG, Bland JM (1999). Treatment allocation in controlled trials: why randomise? BMJ, 318: 1209.
  2. Altman DG, Bland JM (2007). Missing data. BMJ, 334: 424.
  3. Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Sample size slippages in randomised trials: exclusions and the lost and wayward. Lancet, 359: 781-785.
  4. Mills EJ, Chan AW, Wu P et al. (2009). Design, analysis, and presentation of crossover trials. Trials, 10: 27.
  5. Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Allocation concealment in randomised trials: defending against deciphering. Lancet, 359: 614-618.
  6. Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Blinding in randomised trials: hiding who got what. Lancet, 359: 696-700.
  7. Altman DG, Bland JM (2005). Treatment allocation by minimisation. BMJ, 330: 843.

13.3.1.5Blinding and the biases it prevents

Big idea. Knowing who got what changes how people behave, report and score, so every group kept in the dark removes one route for bias.
Picture it as a wine tasting with the labels covered.

Syllabus: Blinding

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 87 · RCTs: randomisation and blinding →

The story in plain words. Blinding keeps people from knowing who received which treatment after allocation. It matters because knowing changes behaviour: patients report differently, clinicians treat differently and raters score differently, often without noticing. Single blind usually means the participant. Double blind adds the clinicians or outcome assessors. Triple blind adds the data analysts or the monitoring committee. These labels are used loosely, so CONSORT 2025 asks authors to name each group that was blinded. Each group blinded closes a different door. Blinded assessors prevent detection bias, also called measurement, ascertainment or observer bias. Blinded clinicians prevent cointervention bias. ((? Clinicians who know a patient is on placebo add benzodiazepines; which group should be blinded? ?)) The treating clinicians, because extra treatment in the placebo arm shrinks the apparent difference.

The people and the evidence. Hróbjartsson and colleagues (2012) gathered trials in which the same patients were assessed by both blinded and unblinded assessors. The unblinded assessors exaggerated odds ratios by about 36% on average. In psychiatry, where outcomes are rating scales, that is a real threat. Day and Altman (2000) and Schulz and Grimes (2002) give the same advice: blind as many groups as possible, state exactly who was blinded, and when patients or therapists cannot be blinded, blind the person who measures the outcome.

From everyday life to the clinic. A wine tasting with the labels covered works because the expensive bottle cannot win on reputation. Uncover the labels and the same wine scores higher. Raters filling in a depression scale behave like tasters. On an inpatient unit, nurses who know which ward has the new aggression protocol may watch that ward more closely, and incidents get recorded differently. In a trauma-focused CBT trial neither patient nor therapist can be blind, so the safeguard is a blinded outcome assessor, with a check on whether they can guess the allocation.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Do not confuse blinding with allocation concealment. Concealment protects the sequence up to allocation and prevents selection bias; blinding acts after allocation and mainly prevents measurement bias. A stem about secrecy after allocation points to blinding. If the stem describes extra treatment given to one arm, think cointervention and blind the clinicians. If it describes ratings or incident counts that depend on who is watching, think detection bias and blind the assessors.

Sources
  1. Eldridge SM, Chan CL, Campbell MJ et al. (2016). CONSORT 2010 statement: extension to randomised pilot and feasibility trials. BMJ, 355: i5239.
  2. Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Generation of allocation sequences in randomised trials: chance, not choice. Lancet, 359: 515-519.
  3. Hróbjartsson A, Thomsen ASS, Emanuelsson F et al. (2012). Observer bias in randomised clinical trials with binary outcomes: systematic review of trials with both blinded and non-blinded outcome assessors. BMJ, 344: e1119.
  4. Kazdin AE (2011). Single-Case Research Designs: Methods for Clinical and Applied Settings, 2nd ed. Oxford University Press.
  5. Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Blinding in randomised trials: hiding who got what. Lancet, 359: 696-700.

13.3.1.6Missing data and who to analyse

Big idea. Randomisation only protects the comparison if everyone randomised is analysed, so every method for missing data is a guess that has to be tested.
Picture it as a class register that keeps every name, even the absent.

Syllabus: Handling missing data: intention to treat, per protocol, LOCF, multiple imputation, best case, worst case and sensitivity analysis

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 98 · Intention-to-treat and missing data →

The story in plain words. Patients leave trials. They feel better, feel worse, get side effects or move house. The question is who to analyse. Intention to treat analyses everyone in the arm they were randomised to, whatever happened next. It keeps the balance randomisation created and estimates the effect of offering the treatment in real life. Per protocol analyses only those who took the treatment as planned. It estimates efficacy under ideal use, but adherent patients differ from non-adherent ones, so it is prone to bias. As-treated analysis groups people by what they actually took and breaks randomisation. In a superiority trial ITT is the primary analysis; in a non-inferiority trial both are reported. ITT still needs outcomes for those who left. Last observation carried forward takes the final score before drop-out and holds it flat. ((? A patient's HAM-D is 20 at week 3 when they leave an 8-week trial; what does LOCF record at week 8? ?)) 20, as in the figure, even though their depression would probably have kept improving.

The people and the evidence. Hollis and Campbell (1999) surveyed published trials and found the term intention to treat was often applied loosely, with some trials still leaving randomised patients out. The label alone is not reassurance: check the numbers randomised against the numbers analysed. Sterne and colleagues (2009) explained multiple imputation: create several plausible complete datasets, analyse each and combine them with Rubin's rules, so the uncertainty about the missing values is carried into the confidence interval. It assumes data are missing at random, that is, explained by what was observed.

From everyday life to the clinic. A class register keeps every name, including the children who were absent; it does not quietly delete them to make attendance look better. ITT is that register. Best case and worst case analyses ask what the absent might have done: best case gives the new arm good outcomes and the control arm poor ones, and worst case reverses it. In an opioid dependence trial, if every drop-out on treatment is assumed to have relapsed and every control drop-out is assumed abstinent, and the benefit survives, attrition cannot explain the result. Repeating the analysis under different assumptions like this is a sensitivity analysis, and an unchanged conclusion means the finding is robust.

Where the exam tries to catch you. When a stem gives 50 versus 50 randomised and some stop treatment, the primary analysis is still 50 versus 50. Completers only, or patients regrouped by what they took, is the wrong answer. LOCF assumes no change after drop-out, ignores the natural course of illness and makes intervals falsely narrow; it is not reliably conservative. Pure pharmacological efficacy among those who took the drug as directed points to per protocol. Sensitivity analysis tests assumptions; subgroup analysis tests kinds of patient.

Sources
  1. Hopewell S, Chan AW, Collins GS et al. (2025). CONSORT 2025 statement: updated guideline for reporting randomised trials. BMJ, 389: e081123.
  2. Bassler D, Briel M, Montori VM et al. (2010). Stopping randomized trials early for benefit and estimation of treatment effects. JAMA, 303: 1180-1187.
  3. Suntharalingam G, Perry MR, Ward S et al. (2006). Cytokine storm in a phase 1 trial of the anti-CD28 monoclonal antibody TGN1412. N Engl J Med, 355: 1018-1028.
  4. Shadish WR, Cook TD, Campbell DT (2002). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference. Houghton Mifflin.

13.3.7Validity, endpoints and trial phases

Big idea. A trial can be true inside its own walls and still not travel to your ward, so ask separately whether it is right and whether it is relevant.
Picture it as a recipe that works in the test kitchen but not at home.

Syllabus: Internal and external validity of trials, explanatory and pragmatic trials, endpoints and early stopping, and clinical trial phases I to IV

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 110 · Trial phases and validity →

The story in plain words. Internal validity asks whether the effect in this trial is real: due to the treatment and not to bias or confounding. It is protected by randomisation, concealment, blinding and complete follow-up. External validity asks whether the result applies to my patients, in my service. An explanatory trial tests efficacy under ideal conditions: selected patients, placebo control, weekly reviews. A pragmatic trial tests effectiveness in routine practice: broad entry, usual clinicians, an active comparator and ITT. PRECIS-2 scores 9 domains along that spectrum. Drugs climb through four phases. Phase I gives a new compound to 20 to 100 people, usually healthy volunteers, for safety and pharmacokinetics; phase II finds the dose in a few hundred patients; phase III runs large comparative RCTs for licensing; phase IV watches tens of thousands after launch. ((? Why are rare harms usually found in phase IV? ?)) A harm at 1 in 10,000 needs about 30,000 patients for a 95% chance of seeing even one case, far more than phase III enrols.

The people and the evidence. Rothwell (2005) argued that trials are often internally sound yet tell clinicians little about whom they apply to, and listed setting, selection, patient characteristics and outcome measures as the questions to ask. Bassler and colleagues (2010) found that trials stopped early for benefit reported larger effects than comparable trials that ran to completion. Fleming and DeMets (1996) warned that surrogate endpoints can mislead: a treatment can move the marker without changing the outcome that matters. In 2006 the TGN1412 phase I trial in London left six healthy volunteers critically ill within hours, a reminder of why phase I is small, staged and closely watched (Suntharalingam et al., 2006).

From everyday life to the clinic. A recipe perfected in a test kitchen, with exact scales and a chef watching, may disappoint at home. The recipe is not wrong; the conditions differ. That is the gap between efficacy and effectiveness. A new antipsychotic trial that excludes substance misuse and physical illness, uses a double-blind placebo and reviews weekly may be internally excellent, yet a district general ward full of comorbid patients sees smaller gains. Growing a trial from 200 to 2,000 participants improves precision, narrowing the confidence interval, but does not remove bias.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Sample size buys precision, not validity: a large biased trial gives a precise wrong answer. Recruitment only from a tertiary unit threatens external validity; poor concealment threatens internal validity. Shorter duration of untreated psychosis standing in for disability at ten years is a surrogate. A trial stopped early for benefit is likely to overestimate the effect. First in human is phase I; post-marketing detection of a rare blood dyscrasia is phase IV.

Sources
  1. Sacks H, Chalmers TC, Smith H (1982). Randomized versus historical controls for clinical trials. Am J Med, 72: 233-240.
  2. Medical Research Council (1948). Streptomycin treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis. BMJ, 2: 769-782.
  3. Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.
  4. Campbell MK, Piaggio G, Elbourne DR, Altman DG (2012). CONSORT 2010 statement: extension to cluster randomised trials. BMJ, 345: e5661.

Category 213.11 · Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials

13.3.1.1The randomised controlled trial and its variants

Big idea. A randomised controlled trial is a fair race: the only systematic difference between the runners is the treatment, so any gap at the finish line can be credited to it.
Picture it as two identical sourdough starters, one fed a new flour.

Syllabus: RCT study

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 87 · RCTs: randomisation and blinding →Research Methods, page 104 · Crossover, cluster and factorial trials →

The story in plain words. Imagine two jars of sourdough starter taken from the same batch. You feed one with a new flour and the other with the usual flour, keep them on the same shelf, and compare how high they rise. Because the jars began identical and lived identical lives, any difference in rise belongs to the flour. That is the whole logic of the randomised controlled trial: make two groups alike in everything except the intervention, then compare outcomes. A trial has a fixed anatomy. Eligible people are identified, consented and sometimes put through a run-in period; they are randomised; each arm receives its intervention; outcomes are measured, ideally blind; and everyone is analysed in the group they were allocated to. The control arm can be placebo, an active comparator, or treatment as usual when withholding proven care would be unethical, as the Declaration of Helsinki requires. In a crossover trial each patient receives both treatments in sequence, separated by a washout, so each person is their own control. Stable personal characteristics such as age and sex cannot confound the comparison, and far fewer patients are needed. ((? Why would a crossover design be useless for a trial with death or cure as the outcome? ?)) Because the outcome cannot be reversed, so there is no second period in which to test the other treatment.

Parallel-group trial against a two-period crossover with washout. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. James Lind compared six remedies for scurvy among sailors in 1747 and reported it in 1753; only the citrus pair recovered. His groups were small and not randomised, but the idea of a concurrent comparison was there. The Medical Research Council streptomycin trial of 1948, designed with Austin Bradford Hill, used random numbers in sealed envelopes and is usually counted as the first properly randomised trial. Pablos-Mendez and colleagues (1998) showed how run-in periods select adherent responders before randomisation. The trial result stays internally valid, but the patients it applies to are a filtered group.

From everyday life to the clinic. A placebo run-in removes people who will not take tablets or who improve on anything; an active run-in removes those who cannot tolerate the drug. Both raise adherence and so power, but your clinic contains exactly the people who were removed. Trial type also changes the sample size. To show equivalence you must prove the difference is smaller than a narrow margin in both directions, which needs far more patients than showing superiority of a large effect. The narrower the margin, the larger the trial.

Two jars from one batch: the logic of a randomised controlled trial. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Questions describe a design and ask you to name it: a treatment-as-usual arm when standard care is the comparator, a run-in when everyone takes the drug before randomisation, a crossover when each patient gets both. The trap is choosing placebo or open control for a usual-care arm. For sample size, remember the ranking: equivalence with a narrow margin needs the most, superiority with a large effect the least. For crossover, the trap is offering it for an irreversible outcome.

Name the design and the control arm: say this, not that. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources

  2. Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Allocation concealment in randomised trials: defending against deciphering. Lancet, 359: 614-618.
  3. Little RJ, D'Agostino R, Cohen ML, et al. (2012). The prevention and treatment of missing data in clinical trials. New England Journal of Medicine, 367: 1355-1360.

13.3.1.4Randomisation and allocation concealment

Big idea. Randomisation lets chance, not anyone's judgement, decide who gets what, so known and unknown prognostic factors are balanced on average.
Picture it as dealing cards face down from a shuffled deck.

Syllabus: Randomisation techniques such as simple, block, stratified, minimisation, cluster, adaptive

The story in plain words. A card dealer who can see the cards can give the aces to friends. Shuffle the deck and deal face down, and nobody can steer the hands. Randomisation is the shuffle; allocation concealment is dealing face down. Together they stop the person recruiting a patient from knowing, or influencing, which arm that patient will join. Its unique gift is that it balances not only the factors you measured but those you never thought of. Matching or statistical adjustment can only deal with known confounders; randomisation deals with unknown ones too. That is why the randomised trial sits above every observational design when the question is whether a treatment works. Simple randomisation is a coin toss for each patient. In small trials it can drift badly out of balance, as the burgundy line in the figure shows. Block randomisation fixes the numbers within each small block, so the arms never differ by more than half a block. Stratified randomisation runs separate blocks within important subgroups such as site or severity, and minimisation assigns each new patient to whichever arm best balances the chosen factors so far. ((? Is allocating by odd or even hospital number randomisation? ?)) No. It is quasi-random and predictable, so recruiters can foresee the allocation.

Running imbalance between arms under simple randomisation and under permuted blocks of four. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Schulz and Grimes (2002) collected the ways clinicians deciphered allocation schemes, from holding envelopes up to a lamp to reading alternation patterns, and showed that trials with inadequate concealment report exaggerated benefits. Pocock and Simon (1975) introduced minimisation, now widely used in multicentre trials with several prognostic factors.

From everyday life to the clinic. Picture a team offering a new mood app only to patients who volunteer, with decliners as controls. Volunteers are usually more motivated and better supported, so they would have done better anyway. Without random allocation, the comparison measures motivation as much as the app. Good methods are computer-generated sequences held centrally, by telephone or web, so the recruiter cannot see the next allocation. Date of birth, day of the week and alternation all fail because they are predictable.

Shuffled and dealt face down: randomisation and allocation concealment. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The commonest question asks which allocation method is least adequate: choose the predictable one, such as hospital number, date of birth or alternation. Coin tossing is crude but genuinely random. The second trap confuses balance at baseline with blinding or intention to treat. Baseline similarity comes from randomisation; blinding and intention to treat protect what happens after it.

Adequate and inadequate allocation methods. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources

13.3.1.6Missing data, non-adherence and intention to treat

Big idea. Analyse everyone in the group they were randomised to, because the people who stop taking a treatment differ from those who persist, and dropping them rebuilds the bias randomisation removed.
Picture it as a school league table that quietly leaves out the pupils who left.

Syllabus: Handling missing data

The story in plain words. A school that excludes pupils who left mid-year from its exam results will look better than it is, because leavers were often struggling. Per-protocol analysis does the same to a trial: it keeps only the people who took the treatment as planned. Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis keeps everyone in the arm they were randomised to, whatever they did afterwards, and so preserves the balance randomisation created. The figure shows why it matters. In the placebo arm alone, adherers relapse at 30% and non-adherers at 50%, although both took the same inert tablet. Adherence is a marker of better prognosis. Strip the non-adherers out of both arms and the drug appears more effective (RR 0.50) than the ITT comparison suggests (RR 0.64). ITT also means that a participant who recovers early and stops attending is still analysed in their arm, and someone who never takes a dose is analysed where they were allocated. ((? A patient randomised to placebo dies before the first dose. Is she excluded from ITT? ?)) No. Everyone randomised is analysed in the allocated arm.

One invented trial analysed two ways, and the adherer effect within the placebo arm. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. The Coronary Drug Project (1980) found that men who took over 80% of their placebo had lower five-year mortality than poor adherers to placebo. It became the classic warning that adherence carries prognosis with it. Little and colleagues (2012), for the US National Research Council, set out how to prevent and handle missing data: design to minimise loss, then use principled methods such as multiple imputation and sensitivity analysis. Simple fixes each carry assumptions. Last observation carried forward assumes nobody would have changed after dropping out; best-case and worst-case analyses bracket the possible answer; complete-case analysis assumes those lost are like those who stayed.

From everyday life to the clinic. In a three-arm crisis-care trial, more patients drop out of the residential arm than the community arm, yet the ITT outcomes do not differ. The honest summary is no demonstrated difference in outcome, with more non-completion in the residential arm. That second fact is a result in its own right: a service people leave is less acceptable. When a paper shows striking benefit only among adherent patients, either the drug works or the characteristics that go with adherence do. The comparison cannot separate the two.

A league table that drops the leavers flatters the school, as per-protocol analysis flatters a drug. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The classic stem compares adherers with non-adherers and asks what can be concluded. The answer always names adherence-related factors as an alternative explanation; never accept that the drug is proven. Watch for statements that ITT distorts randomisation (it protects it), that prognosis is similar in adherers and non-adherers (it is not), and that people who recover early are excluded (they are kept).

Under intention to treat, every randomised participant stays in the allocated arm. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Hrobjartsson A, Gotzsche PC (2001). Is the placebo powerless? An analysis of clinical trials comparing placebo with no treatment. New England Journal of Medicine, 344: 1594-1602.
  2. Donner A, Klar N (2000). Design and Analysis of Cluster Randomization Trials in Health Research. Arnold.
  3. Medical Research Council (1948). Streptomycin treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis. BMJ, 2: 769-782.

13.3.1.8Relative risk, relative risk reduction and their confidence intervals

Big idea. Relative measures describe how much a treatment changes risk compared with control; sample size does not move the estimate, it only narrows the interval around it.
Picture it as a sale that is always 30 per cent off, whatever the price tag.

Syllabus: Relative risk (with relative risk reduction, 13.3.1.12)

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 15 · Absolute and relative risk →

The story in plain words. A shop sign saying 30 per cent off tells you the proportion saved, not the money. On a £10 shirt you save £3; on a £1000 sofa you save £300. Relative risk reduction (RRR) is that sign. It tells you what fraction of the baseline risk the treatment removes, but not how much risk there was to remove. From a 2 x 2 table: EER is the event rate on treatment and CER the event rate on control. Relative risk, RR = EER / CER, has its null value at 1. RRR is 1 minus RR, or ARR / CER, and its null value is 0. If 24 of 200 patients are readmitted after an intervention and 40 of 200 after usual care, RR is 0.12 / 0.20 = 0.60 and RRR is 40%. The figure shows the same RR of 0.70 from trials of 50, 150 and 1500 per arm. The point estimate never moves, because the event rates are identical; only the confidence interval narrows. ((? Which of the three trials is statistically significant at the 5% level? ?)) Only the largest, the one whose interval excludes 1 on the RR scale and 0 on the RRR scale.

The same relative risk of 0.70 from trials of three sizes, on the RR scale and the RRR scale. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Laupacis, Sackett and Roberts (1988) argued that relative measures hide the absolute size of benefit and proposed the number needed to treat instead. Spruance and colleagues (2004) explained the hazard ratio, the relative measure for time-to-event data: an average ratio of instantaneous event rates over follow-up, using who is still at risk at each moment. The Users' Guides teach that a confidence interval shows the range of true effects compatible with the data, and that p = 0.05 places one end of the 95% interval exactly on the null value.

From everyday life to the clinic. A trial reports an RRR for death of 10% with a 95% CI from minus 25% to 35%. The data are compatible with a substantial benefit and with substantial harm, so the trial has not settled the question. It does not mean 10% of patients benefit, and it says nothing about how individual patients spread around the average. A trial reporting that 28% of controls and 20% of treated patients were readmitted has treated readmission as a dichotomous outcome. Those figures are event rates, not risk reductions.

The same 30% off saves very different amounts: relative versus absolute. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Null values decide many questions: 1 for any ratio (RR, OR, HR), 0 for any difference or reduction (ARR, RRR, mean difference). A CI for RRR must exclude 0, not 1. Other traps: thinking a larger sample changes the point estimate, reading a CI as the range of individual responses, and calling an event rate a risk reduction.

Null values: 1 for ratios, 0 for differences and reductions. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Lind J (1753). A Treatise of the Scurvy. Edinburgh: Sands, Murray and Cochran.
  2. Straus SE, Glasziou P, Richardson WS, Haynes RB (2019). Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM, 5th ed. Elsevier.
  3. Guyatt G, Sackett D, Taylor DW, et al. (1986). Determining optimal therapy: randomized trials in individual patients. New England Journal of Medicine, 314: 889-892.

Challenge 1 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1
Referral orderDate referredAllocated to

36 MarLithium plus antidepressant

717 MarLithium plus antidepressant
819 MarAntidepressant alone
Allocation log for the first eight patients referred. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In a trial of adding lithium to an antidepressant for resistant depression, patients are allocated in strict order of referral. The allocation log shows the first eight patients. How is this study best described?
  1. Randomised controlled trial
  2. Cluster randomised trial
  3. Factorial trial
  4. Crossover trial
  5. Non-randomised controlled trial
Show the working
Answer: E Non-randomised controlled trial

Alternation looks systematic and fair, but because the next allocation is known, recruiters can influence who is enrolled when. CONSORT and Cochrane class alternation as quasi-random, so the trial is a non-randomised controlled trial.

The log shows the pattern: odd referrals get the combination and even referrals the antidepressant alone, so the ninth allocation is known before the ninth patient arrives. Because the next allocation is predictable, the recruiter can steer patients. That makes alternation quasi-random and the trial a non-randomised controlled trial.

Rule: Alternation gives a controlled trial, but not a randomised one.
Trap: Calling alternation a form of randomisation.

Source: Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Generation of allocation sequences in randomised trials: chance, not choice. Lancet, 359: 515-519.

Challenge 2 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.4
After participant5101520
App arm471114
Control arm1346
Difference3478
Arm sizes in a simulated run of coin-toss allocation for the first 20 participants. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A small trial of a smartphone app for bipolar disorder will recruit 60 participants over 18 months. The investigators want the two arms to stay close to equal in size throughout recruitment. The table shows a simulated run of coin-toss allocation for the first 20 participants. Which method best achieves their aim?
  1. Simple randomisation by coin toss
  2. Block randomisation
  3. Cluster randomisation
  4. Allocation by day of the week
  5. Stratified randomisation by site without blocks
Show the working
Answer: B Block randomisation

In blocks of 4, each block contains two of each allocation in random order (for example ABBA, BABA). Arm sizes never differ by more than two. Varying block sizes randomly makes the sequence harder to guess.

The table shows the problem: after 20 coin tosses the arms stand at 14 v 6. Blocks of 4 would have left them at 10 v 10. Blocks of 4 keep the arms within two of each other at all times. Vary block sizes so recruiters cannot predict the last allocation in a block.

Rule: Equal arm sizes throughout = block randomisation.
Trap: Choosing simple randomisation in a small trial, where chance alone can leave the arms unequal.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1999). How to randomise. BMJ, 319: 703-704.

Challenge 3 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.6
Flow of participants through a randomised trial of depot versus oral antipsychotic medication. 100 randomised, 50 to each arm; 9 (depot) and 14 (oral) stopped their allocated treatment and switched to the other formulation. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A trial randomises 100 patients with schizophrenia, 50 to depot and 50 to oral medication. During the trial, 9 in the depot arm and 14 in the oral arm stop their allocated treatment and switch to the other formulation (figure). Which analysis should be the primary one reported?
  1. 41 versus 36: those who completed treatment
  2. 50 versus 50: everyone as randomised
  3. 55 versus 45: patients regrouped by the formulation they ended on
  4. 41 versus 50: completers in the depot arm against all in the oral arm
  5. 23 switchers compared with 77 who stayed on their allocation
Show the working
Answer: B 50 versus 50: everyone as randomised

Working: depot completers 50 minus 9 = 41; oral completers 50 minus 14 = 36. Analysing only these 77 drops patients for reasons linked to the treatment. Regrouping by the formulation taken gives 41 + 14 = 55 versus 36 + 9 = 45, an as-treated analysis. ITT keeps all 100 in their original groups, preserving comparability, and needs a plan for missing outcomes.

The flow diagram shows 41 and 36 completers, but the primary analysis keeps all 50 versus 50. Every randomised patient stays in their arm.

Rule: Primary analysis = intention-to-treat, everyone as randomised.
Trap: Reporting completers only.

Source: Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.

Challenge 4 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.6
Flow of participants through a randomised trial of depot versus oral antipsychotic medication. 100 randomised, 50 to each arm; 9 (depot) and 14 (oral) stopped their allocated treatment and switched to the other formulation. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the same figure, what is the term for analysing all 50 patients in each arm in the group to which they were randomised, including the 9 and 14 who switched, whatever treatment they actually received?
  1. Intention-to-treat analysis
  2. As-treated analysis
  3. Per-protocol analysis
  4. Subgroup analysis
  5. Completer analysis
Show the working
Answer: A Intention-to-treat analysis

ITT preserves the balance created by randomisation and estimates the effect of offering a treatment in practice, including non-adherence. It tends to be conservative in superiority trials.

Analysing all 50 in each arm, including the 9 and 14 who switched, is intention to treat. As-treated would regroup them by what they took.

Rule: As randomised = intention-to-treat.
Trap: Confusing ITT with as-treated.

Source: Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.

Challenge 5 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.7
Trial featureThis trial
Who can enteradults with schizophrenia; substance misuse and physical illness excluded
Comparatorplacebo, double blind
Follow-upweekly review for 12 weeks
Settingtwo specialist research units
Primary outcomechange in PANSS score at 12 weeks
Summary of the trial design. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The card summarises a trial of a new antipsychotic. Which description best fits this trial?
  1. Pragmatic trial: high external validity, testing effectiveness
  2. Explanatory trial: high internal validity, limited external validity
  3. Explanatory trial: limited internal validity, high external validity
  4. Pragmatic trial: limited internal validity, testing efficacy
  5. Phase IV study: post-marketing surveillance in routine care
Show the working
Answer: B Explanatory trial: high internal validity, limited external validity

Selective samples, blinding, placebo and close monitoring all raise internal validity and test efficacy under ideal conditions. Real patients have comorbidity, know what they take and are seen less often, so effects in practice may be smaller.

Every row of the card (narrow entry, placebo, weekly review, specialist units) sits at the explanatory end of the PRECIS-2 spectrum. The trade-off is high internal validity for limited external validity.

Rule: Explanatory trial features improve internal validity but reduce generalisability.
Trap: Reversing the trade-off: thinking tight control lowers internal validity.

Source: Rothwell PM (2005). External validity of randomised controlled trials: "to whom do the results of this trial apply?" Lancet, 365: 82-93.

ArmRandomised, nDid not complete, n (%)Good outcome, n (%)
Crisis house6024 (40%)17 (28%)

Standard CMHT care6015 (25%)15 (25%)
Total1805145
Three-arm crisis-care trial at 12 months; good outcome analysed by original allocation (no significant difference). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A three-arm RCT across four NHS trusts randomised 180 adults in a mental health crisis to a residential crisis house (n = 60), intensive home treatment (n = 60) or standard community mental health team (CMHT) care with no added specialist input (n = 60). Follow-up was 12 months. Twenty-four crisis-house, 12 home-treatment and 15 CMHT participants did not complete their allocated care. A predefined good outcome was reached by 17 of 60 (28%, crisis house), 13 of 60 (22%, home treatment) and 15 of 60 (25%, CMHT). Analysis by original allocation found no statistically significant difference in good outcome between arms. The CMHT arm, which received standard care with no added specialist input, is best described as
  1. Placebo arm
  2. Treatment-as-usual arm
  3. Waiting-list arm
  4. Sham-intervention arm
  5. Run-in arm
Show the working
Answer: B Treatment-as-usual arm

Comparing a new service with the care normally provided makes the comparator a treatment as usual arm.

No dummy treatment was given (placebo), nobody was waiting for the intervention (waiting list), nothing was imitated (sham), and a run-in precedes randomisation.

Rule: Usual care as the comparator = treatment as usual (TAU).
Trap: Calling any non-intervention arm a placebo arm.
What each type of control arm receives. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Zwarenstein M, Treweek S, Gagnier JJ, et al. (2008). Improving the reporting of pragmatic trials: an extension of the CONSORT statement. BMJ, 337: a2390.

Challenge 7 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.4
How the two groups in the app evaluation were formed. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A community team offers a new mood-tracking app to 40 patients who volunteer for it; 40 patients who decline continue usual care. The figure shows how the groups were formed. At 12 weeks the app group has lower depression scores on a validated scale. Which essential element of a sound treatment evaluation is missing?
  1. A defined outcome measure
  2. Random allocation to the groups
  3. An intervention
  4. A comparison group
  5. A follow-up period
Show the working
Answer: B Random allocation to the groups

The patients chose their own group. Volunteers for a new app tend to be more motivated, better supported or less unwell, and those same traits predict lower depression scores.

Only random allocation cuts the link between patient characteristics and group. The study already has an outcome measure, an intervention, a comparison group and follow-up.

Rule: Without randomisation, self-selection biases group comparison.
Trap: Accepting a comparison group as adequate when the patients chose their own group.
Self-selection: motivation drives both the choice and the outcome. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.

Baseline characteristics by allocated arm in the three-arm crisis-care trial. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A three-arm RCT across four NHS trusts randomised 180 adults in a mental health crisis to a residential crisis house (n = 60), intensive home treatment (n = 60) or standard community mental health team (CMHT) care with no added specialist input (n = 60). Follow-up was 12 months. Twenty-four crisis-house, 12 home-treatment and 15 CMHT participants did not complete their allocated care. A predefined good outcome was reached by 17 of 60 (28%, crisis house), 13 of 60 (22%, home treatment) and 15 of 60 (25%, CMHT). Analysis by original allocation found no statistically significant difference in good outcome between arms. Baseline age, sex, illness severity and previous admissions were similar across the three arms (table). This similarity is best explained by
  1. Blinding of outcome assessors
  2. Intention-to-treat analysis
  3. Random allocation
  4. Recruitment from four trusts
  5. Similar completion rates across arms
Show the working
Answer: C Random allocation

Random allocation acts at the moment patients enter the trial, so known and unknown prognostic factors are spread evenly and the baseline table looks alike across arms.

Blinding and intention to treat protect what happens after allocation. Recruiting from four trusts helps generalisability. Completion rates were not similar (24, 12 and 15 non-completers) and in any case come after baseline.

Rule: Balanced baseline tables are the fingerprint of successful randomisation.
Trap: Crediting blinding or ITT for baseline balance.
The 180 participants by allocated arm: previous admissions (counts from the baseline table) and an unmeasured factor, both spread evenly by chance. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Schulz KF, Altman DG, Moher D, for the CONSORT Group (2010). CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ, 340: c332.

Three-arm crisis-care trial at 12 months; good outcome analysed by original allocation (no significant difference). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A three-arm RCT across four NHS trusts randomised 180 adults in a mental health crisis to a residential crisis house (n = 60), intensive home treatment (n = 60) or standard community mental health team (CMHT) care with no added specialist input (n = 60). Follow-up was 12 months. Twenty-four crisis-house, 12 home-treatment and 15 CMHT participants did not complete their allocated care. A predefined good outcome was reached by 17 of 60 (28%, crisis house), 13 of 60 (22%, home treatment) and 15 of 60 (25%, CMHT). Analysis by original allocation found no statistically significant difference in good outcome between arms. Although more crisis-house participants failed to complete, all participants were analysed in the arm to which they were originally assigned. This is
  1. Intention-to-treat analysis
  2. Per-protocol analysis
  3. As-treated analysis
  4. Last observation carried forward
  5. Sensitivity analysis
Show the working
Answer: A Intention-to-treat analysis

Analysing every participant in the arm to which they were originally assigned, whatever happened next, is intention-to-treat analysis.

Per-protocol analysis keeps only completers (36, 48 and 45 here); as-treated analysis regroups by what was received. Both can break randomisation.

Rule: Analysed as randomised = ITT.
Trap: Confusing ITT with per-protocol analysis.
Who is analysed under ITT and under per-protocol. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.

Challenge 10 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.8
GroupReadmitted within one year
Placebo30%
Treatment22%
Results as reported in the trial abstract. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A trial reports that 30% of the placebo group and 22% of the treatment group were readmitted within a year (table). Which statement is valid?
  1. The treatment is 22% effective
  2. Readmission was handled as a dichotomous outcome
  3. The relative risk of readmission on treatment is above 1
  4. The treatment prevents 30% of readmissions
  5. The absolute risk reduction is 22%
Show the working
Answer: B Readmission was handled as a dichotomous outcome

Results given as the percentage of patients with or without an event treat the outcome as a yes or no (dichotomous) variable.

The two figures are event rates, not effects. From them: ARR 8 points, RR 22 / 30 = 0.73 and RRR 27%. The RR is below 1, so readmission is less likely on treatment.

Rule: Event rates are proportions of a dichotomous outcome; effect measures are derived from them.
Trap: Reading an event rate as a risk reduction.
Event rates of a yes or no outcome, and the measures derived from them. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Guyatt G, Rennie D, Meade MO, Cook DJ (2015). Users' Guides to the Medical Literature: Essentials of Evidence-Based Clinical Practice, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill / JAMA.

Challenge 11 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.8
Relative risk reduction for death with its 95% confidence interval. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A large multicentre RCT reports a relative risk reduction for death of 12% (95% CI minus 30% to 41%), shown in the figure. The most valid conclusion is
  1. 30% of patients will be harmed by the treatment
  2. The maximum benefit achievable with the treatment is 41%
  3. 95% of patients will respond within minus 30% to 41%
  4. The treatment has been shown to be ineffective
  5. The trial has not settled whether the treatment helps or harms
Show the working
Answer: E The trial has not settled whether the treatment helps or harms

The interval runs from a 30% increase in risk to a 41% reduction. Both ends would change practice in opposite directions, so the trial is inconclusive.

A confidence interval describes uncertainty about one average effect. It does not say what share of patients are harmed or helped, and it does not prove that the treatment is ineffective.

Rule: A wide CI spanning important harm and important benefit is inconclusive.
Trap: Treating 'non-significant' as 'proven no effect'.
An interval compatible with important harm and important benefit. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1995). Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. BMJ, 311: 485.

Challenge 12 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.8
Cumulative incidence of new-onset diabetes on two antipsychotics, with censoring ticks and numbers at risk. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
An investigator wants one relative measure comparing the instantaneous rate of new-onset diabetes between two antipsychotics over a 3-year follow-up, using the timing of each event and the number still at risk. The figure shows the curves he wants to summarise. The measure is the
  1. Odds ratio
  2. Standardised mean difference
  3. Number needed to harm
  4. Kappa
  5. Hazard ratio
Show the working
Answer: E Hazard ratio

When the timing of events matters and people are followed for different lengths of time, the relative measure is the hazard ratio, usually from Cox regression.

It compares instantaneous event rates among those still at risk and assumes the ratio is constant over time (proportional hazards). Odds ratios and NNH ignore timing; SMD and kappa answer other questions.

Rule: Time-to-event comparison = hazard ratio (from Cox regression).
Trap: Choosing the odds ratio for survival data.
Proportional hazards: a constant ratio of event rates over time, with numbers at risk. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Spruance SL, Reid JE, Grace M, Samore M (2004). Hazard ratio in clinical trials. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, 48: 2787-2792.

Three-arm crisis-care trial at 12 months; good outcome analysed by original allocation (no significant difference). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A three-arm RCT across four NHS trusts randomised 180 adults in a mental health crisis to a residential crisis house (n = 60), intensive home treatment (n = 60) or standard community mental health team (CMHT) care with no added specialist input (n = 60). Follow-up was 12 months. Twenty-four crisis-house, 12 home-treatment and 15 CMHT participants did not complete their allocated care. A predefined good outcome was reached by 17 of 60 (28%, crisis house), 13 of 60 (22%, home treatment) and 15 of 60 (25%, CMHT). Analysis by original allocation found no statistically significant difference in good outcome between arms. In the standard CMHT arm, what was the risk of NOT achieving the predefined good outcome?
  1. 0.25
  2. 0.33
  3. 0.75
  4. 1.33
  5. 3.0
Show the working
Answer: C 0.75

The CMHT arm had 15 of 60 with a good outcome (25%), so 45 of 60 did not achieve it.

The risk of NOT achieving it is 45 / 60 = 0.75. Risk divides by everyone in the group; odds divide by those without the event (45 / 15 = 3).

Rule: Risk of non-event = 1 minus risk of event.
Trap: Answering with the success rate or the odds.
Risk of the named event, not its complement or its odds. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Guyatt G, Rennie D, Meade MO, Cook DJ (2015). Users' Guides to the Medical Literature: Essentials of Evidence-Based Clinical Practice, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill / JAMA.

Challenge 14 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.8
ArmReadmitted, nNot readmitted, nTotal, n
Discharge-support intervention30220250
Usual discharge care40210250

Readmission within one year after discharge. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Over one year, 30 of 250 patients receiving a new discharge-support intervention are readmitted, compared with 40 of 250 receiving usual discharge care. Using the table, what is the relative risk of readmission with the intervention?
  1. 0.04
  2. 0.25
  3. 1.33
  4. 25
  5. 0.75
Show the working
Answer: E 0.75

EER = 30 / 250 = 0.12; CER = 40 / 250 = 0.16. RR = 0.12 / 0.16 = 0.75.

The same table gives RRR 0.25, ARR 0.04 and NNT 25. Read which one the question asks for.

Rule: RR = EER / CER.
Trap: Choosing the NNT or ARR from the same data set.
Four measures from one table. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Guyatt G, Rennie D, Meade MO, Cook DJ (2015). Users' Guides to the Medical Literature: Essentials of Evidence-Based Clinical Practice, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill / JAMA.

Challenge 15 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.8
ArmReadmitted, nNot readmitted, nTotal, n
Discharge-support intervention30220250
Usual discharge care40210250
Total70430500
Readmission within one year after discharge. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the same data (readmission 30 of 250 with the intervention, 40 of 250 with usual care), by what proportion does the intervention reduce the risk of readmission?
  1. 0.04
  2. 0.25
  3. 0.12
  4. 0.75
  5. 1.33
Show the working
Answer: B 0.25

RRR expresses the reduction as a fraction of the control risk: ARR / CER = 0.04 / 0.16 = 0.25, or 1 minus RR = 1 minus 0.75.

0.04 is the absolute reduction, 0.12 the event rate on the intervention, 0.75 the RR and 1.33 its inverse.

Rule: RRR = 1 minus RR = ARR / CER.
Trap: Answering with the ARR when asked for the proportional reduction.
Relative risk reduction as a share of the control risk. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Guyatt G, Rennie D, Meade MO, Cook DJ (2015). Users' Guides to the Medical Literature: Essentials of Evidence-Based Clinical Practice, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill / JAMA.

Challenge 16 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.13
Responses to the statement "The support scheme helped me cope with the pressures of work", by scheme. 2023 cohort: 124 of 200 responded (62%). 2025 cohort: 86 of 210 responded (41%). Report text: "68% of doctors in the group scheme agreed or strongly agreed, compared with 50% under one-to-one mentoring." Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A mental health trust replaced its one-to-one mentoring scheme for resident doctors with a new group-based peer-support model. The wellbeing lead surveyed the 2023 intake about the old scheme at the end of their year, and the 2025 intake about the new scheme at the end of theirs. Satisfaction was recorded on a 5-point Likert item (figure). What was the main purpose of this evaluation?
  1. To compare the effectiveness of two support models for resident doctors
  2. To measure the prevalence of burnout among resident doctors
  3. To compare survey response rates between two intakes
  4. To validate a new 5-point Likert scale
  5. To test whether peer support reduces sickness absence
Show the working
Answer: A To compare the effectiveness of two support models for resident doctors

The study puts two support models side by side and asks which one doctors found more helpful. Response rates and the Likert format are features of the method, not the purpose. Identifying the aim first helps you judge whether the design can answer it.

In the exam, name the aim from what is being compared before reading the options. Here the comparison is scheme against scheme, so the aim is effectiveness.

Rule: Name the aim from the comparison being made: scheme versus scheme.
Trap: Choosing a method detail (response rate) as the aim.
What the study doesWhat that tells youAim or method?
Compares the old scheme with the new schemewhich scheme helped doctors moreAim
Reports response rates (62% and 41%)how representative the replies areMethod detail
Uses one 5-point Likert itemhow satisfaction was recordedMethod detail
Surveys two intakes two years apartwho was compared, and whenDesign
Name the aim from what is being compared.

Source: Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.

Challenge 17 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.13
Responses to the statement "The support scheme helped me cope with the pressures of work", by scheme. 2023 cohort: 124 of 200 responded (62%). 2025 cohort: 86 of 210 responded (41%). Report text: "68% of doctors in the group scheme agreed or strongly agreed, compared with 50% under one-to-one mentoring." Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the same figure, which statement correctly describes which doctors experienced which scheme?
  1. The 2025 intake had one-to-one mentoring and the 2023 intake had group peer support
  2. Both intakes received both schemes in sequence
  3. Each intake was split at random between the two schemes
  4. The 2023 intake had one-to-one mentoring and the 2025 intake had group peer support
  5. The 2025 intake received no scheme and acted as the control group
Show the working
Answer: D The 2023 intake had one-to-one mentoring and the 2025 intake had group peer support

Reading the legend first avoids reversing the groups. The 2023 intake (teal bars) had one-to-one mentoring and the 2025 intake (navy bars) had group peer support. Each cohort answered about its own scheme only.

Read the legend before the bars. Each intake answered about its own scheme only, which is exactly why the comparison is historical.

Rule: Check the legend: earlier cohort, old scheme; later cohort, new scheme.
Trap: Swapping the groups by reading the bars without the legend.

Source: Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.

Challenge 18 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.13
Responses to the statement "The support scheme helped me cope with the pressures of work", by scheme. 2023 cohort: 124 of 200 responded (62%). 2025 cohort: 86 of 210 responded (41%). Report text: "68% of doctors in the group scheme agreed or strongly agreed, compared with 50% under one-to-one mentoring." Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the same figure, what percentage of doctors in the group peer-support scheme strongly agreed with the statement?
  1. 16%
  2. 40%
  3. 28%
  4. 50%
  5. 68%
Show the working
Answer: C 28%

The report text collapses two categories: 40% agree plus 28% strongly agree gives 68%. The question asks only about strongly agree, which is 28%. Collapsing Likert categories can make differences look larger or smaller than the full distribution shows.

Strongly agree for the group scheme is the single navy bar at 28. The 68% in the report combines agree and strongly agree.

Rule: Read the single category asked for, not the collapsed figure in the text.
Trap: Quoting the 68% headline figure.

Source: Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.

Challenge 19 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.2
A man with longstanding generalised anxiety wants to know whether propranolol actually helps his tremor during presentations. Look at the timeline of his 12 weeks: each two-week pack holds either propranolol or an identical placebo, and he rates his symptoms daily. What is this design?
  1. n of 1 trial
  2. Single-subject ABAB design
  3. Case report
  4. Crossover trial in a population
  5. Uncontrolled before-and-after study
Show the working
Answer: A n of 1 trial

An n of 1 trial is a multiple crossover in a single patient. Randomising the order and blinding both parties reduce bias. The result answers whether this treatment works for this patient.

The timeline shows the signature: three pairs of identical packs, the order randomised within each pair, both parties blind, and daily ratings in one person. The answer applies to this man and his tremor, not to everyone with anxiety.

Rule: One patient, randomised blinded switches of active and placebo = n of 1 trial.
Trap: Confusing n of 1 with an ABAB behavioural design.

Source: Guyatt G, Sackett D, Taylor DW et al. (1986). Determining optimal therapy: randomized trials in individual patients. N Engl J Med, 314: 889-892.

Challenge 20 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.6.6
Forty patients with chronic insomnia take part in the trial shown in the timetable. What is the purpose of the two weeks without study tablets?
  1. To allow blinding of the outcome assessor
  2. To reduce carry-over of the first treatment into the second period
  3. To increase the external validity of the trial
  4. To allow allocation concealment
  5. To reduce regression to the mean
Show the working
Answer: B To reduce carry-over of the first treatment into the second period

In a crossover trial each patient acts as their own control, so fewer participants are needed. The price is carry-over (lingering effects of the first treatment) and period effects (patients change over time). A washout, plus testing for period by treatment interaction, addresses these.

In the timetable, weeks 4 to 6 separate the two treatment periods in both groups. That gap is the washout. Washout protects the second period from the first. Without it, a difference between periods could be leftover drug rather than the new treatment.

Rule: Crossover needs a washout to limit carry-over.
Trap: Thinking the gap is about blinding.

Source: Mills EJ, Chan AW, Wu P et al. (2009). Design, analysis, and presentation of crossover trials. Trials, 10: 27.

Challenge 21 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.6.4
ParticipantFirst randomisationSecond randomisationGroup

P03SertralineUsual activitysertraline alone
P04PlaceboExerciseexercise alone
P05PlaceboUsual activityneither
P06SertralineExerciseboth
Planned: 50 per group, 200 in total.
Randomisation record for the first six participants. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A trial of depression in older adults randomises each participant twice: first to sertraline or placebo, then to a supervised exercise programme or usual activity. The record shows the first six participants. What is this design?
  1. Factorial (2 x 2) trial
  2. Cluster randomised trial
  3. Crossover trial
  4. Adaptive platform trial
  5. Stratified randomised trial
Show the working
Answer: A Factorial (2 x 2) trial

A factorial trial answers two questions for roughly the price of one, provided the interventions do not interact. If they do interact, the trial needs to be powered to detect that interaction, which needs a much larger sample.

The record shows two independent randomisations producing four groups: both, sertraline alone, exercise alone and neither. Four groups from two separate randomisations is the signature of a 2 x 2 factorial. Each main effect is estimated using all participants.

Rule: Two interventions, four groups (A, B, A + B, neither) = factorial trial.
Trap: Calling it a four-arm parallel trial and missing the factorial structure.

Source: Montgomery AA, Peters TJ, Little P (2003). Design, analysis and presentation of factorial randomised controlled trials. BMC Med Res Methodol, 3: 26.

Challenge 22 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.6.2
Service 1Service 2Both
Families approached342660
Families consented141024
Still in the study at 6 months11718
Sessions delivered as planned92 of 112 (82%)59 of 80 (74%)151 of 192 (79%)
Results of the small study in two services. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Before a large trial of a family intervention in early psychosis, a team runs a small study in two services to check how many families can be recruited, how many stay in, and whether the session protocol works. The table shows its results. Which statement about this study is correct?
  1. It tests feasibility of recruitment, retention and procedures, and is not powered for efficacy
  2. A significant result would make the main trial unnecessary
  3. It should be powered to detect a clinically important effect
  4. It is a phase IV study
  5. It must use a crossover design
Show the working
Answer: A It tests feasibility of recruitment, retention and procedures, and is not powered for efficacy

Pilot and feasibility studies estimate recruitment and retention rates, test procedures and outcome measures, and give data for sample size calculations. Hypothesis tests of efficacy are discouraged because the study is underpowered and effect estimates are imprecise.

The table answers feasibility questions only: 24 of 60 families consented (40%), 18 of 24 stayed to 6 months (75%) and 151 of 192 sessions ran as planned (79%). None of these numbers tests whether the intervention works. Pilot results guide the main trial; they do not test the hypothesis. Treat any efficacy estimate from a pilot as imprecise.

Rule: Pilot = can the trial be done, not does the treatment work.
Trap: Over-interpreting an effect size from a pilot.
Pilot or feasibility studyMain (definitive) trial
Questioncan the trial be done?does the treatment work?
Measuresrecruitment, retention, fidelity, outcome measuresprespecified primary outcome
Sizesmall; not powered for efficacyfrom a sample size calculation
Effect estimateimprecise; no hypothesis testthe answer
This study24 of 60 consented (40%); 18 of 24 retained (75%)uses these rates to plan recruitment
Two different questions, two different studies.

Source: Eldridge SM, Chan CL, Campbell MJ et al. (2016). CONSORT 2010 statement: extension to randomised pilot and feasibility trials. BMJ, 355: i5239.

Challenge 23 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.6.1

HAM-D recorded25232120no visitno visitno visitno visitno visit

Trial record for one patient who left after the week 3 visit. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In an 8-week antidepressant trial, the record shows one patient who left after the week 3 visit. What method of handling missing data has produced the week 8 value in the analysis dataset?
  1. Multiple imputation
  2. Worst-case analysis
  3. Complete case analysis
  4. Last observation carried forward
  5. Mixed-effects modelling
Show the working
Answer: D Last observation carried forward

LOCF is simple and keeps everyone in the analysis. It assumes the score would have stayed the same after drop-out, which is rarely true.

In the record, the last observed HAM-D score (20 at week 3) becomes the week 8 value. The single score carried forward from week 3 is the signature of LOCF. It keeps the patient in the analysis at the cost of a strong assumption.

Rule: Last value copied to the end = LOCF.
Trap: Confusing LOCF, a single imputation, with multiple imputation.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (2007). Missing data. BMJ, 334: 424.

Challenge 24 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.6.4
ArmRandomisedAbstinentRelapsedOutcome missing
New treatment150904515
Control150459312
Total30013513827
Opioid dependence trial: abstinence at 6 months by arm. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The table shows a trial of a new treatment for opioid dependence. In one sensitivity analysis, all 15 missing outcomes in the new treatment arm are counted as abstinent and all 12 missing outcomes in the control arm are counted as relapsed. What is this called?
  1. Worst-case analysis
  2. Per-protocol analysis
  3. Multiple imputation
  4. Best-case analysis
  5. Complete case analysis
Show the working
Answer: D Best-case analysis

Best-case and worst-case analyses set the extreme limits of what missing data could do. If both point the same way, the conclusion is robust. If they disagree, missing data could change the answer.

With the table, this gives 105/150 (70%) against 45/150 (30%), a difference of 40 points: the most favourable result the missing data could produce for the new treatment. Good outcomes assumed for the new arm and poor for control is the best case. It sets the upper limit of what missing data could do.

Rule: Best case favours the new arm; worst case penalises it.
Trap: Swapping the definitions of best and worst case.

Source: Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Sample size slippages in randomised trials: exclusions and the lost and wayward. Lancet, 359: 781-785.

Challenge 25 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.8
StagePatients exposedCases of the blood dyscrasia
Before licensing: randomised comparative trials3,0000
First two years after licensing: Yellow Card reports and registries60,0008
Exposure and cases at each stage. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
After licensing, a new antipsychotic is monitored through spontaneous reporting and registries. The table shows exposure and cases of a rare blood dyscrasia before and after licensing. Which phase of evaluation detected the 8 cases?
  1. Phase I
  2. Phase IV
  3. Phase II
  4. Phase III
  5. Pilot phase
Show the working
Answer: B Phase IV

Phase III trials usually include a few thousand patients at most, so harms with a frequency below about 1 in 1,000 are often missed. Phase IV relies on Yellow Card reporting, registries and observational studies.

In the table, 3,000 patients in the licensing trials produced no cases; by the rule of three that only rules out a risk above about 1 in 1,000. Eight cases in 60,000 is about 1 in 7,500, a risk the trials could easily miss. Rare harms need tens of thousands of exposures to appear. That is why post-marketing surveillance is phase IV.

Rule: Rare adverse effects found after licensing = phase IV.
Trap: Expecting phase III to detect rare harms.

Source: Friedman LM, Furberg CD, DeMets DL, Reboussin DM, Granger CB (2015). Fundamentals of Clinical Trials, 5th ed. Springer.

Challenge 26 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1
Responses to the statement "The support scheme helped me cope with the pressures of work", by scheme. 2023 cohort: 124 of 200 responded (62%). 2025 cohort: 86 of 210 responded (41%). Report text: "68% of doctors in the group scheme agreed or strongly agreed, compared with 50% under one-to-one mentoring." Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the same figure, how is this design best described?
  1. Uncontrolled before-and-after study of one cohort
  2. Non-randomised comparison with a historical control group
  3. Cluster randomised trial
  4. Crossover trial
  5. Case-control study
Show the working
Answer: B Non-randomised comparison with a historical control group

Historical controls are a different group treated at an earlier time. They differ from the new group in many ways besides the intervention: intake, rota pressures, pandemic effects and survey timing. Historically controlled studies tend to exaggerate the benefit of the new intervention (Sacks et al., 1982).

Different intakes in different years are different people, so this is not before-and-after. Nobody was randomised, and the earlier intake supplies a historical control.

Rule: Earlier cohort on old care versus later cohort on new care = historically controlled study.
Trap: Calling any old-versus-new comparison a before-and-after study.

Source: Sacks H, Chalmers TC, Smith H (1982). Randomized versus historical controls for clinical trials. Am J Med, 72: 233-240.

Challenge 27 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1
FeatureDrug ADrug B

Evaluation summary, two years of admissions with agitation in delirium. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A general hospital adds a new antipsychotic, drug B, to its formulary alongside the established drug A for agitation in delirium. Over two years clinicians choose freely between the two drugs, and the evaluation team then compares length of stay between patients given A and patients given B. The table summarises the two groups. How is this design best described?
  1. Randomised controlled trial
  2. Case-control study
  3. Crossover trial
  4. Quasi-experimental (non-randomised) comparison
  5. n of 1 trial
Show the working
Answer: D Quasi-experimental (non-randomised) comparison

Large numbers do not replace randomisation. When clinicians choose, sicker or older patients may be steered towards one drug, so differences in length of stay may reflect who got the drug rather than the drug itself. This is confounding by indication.

The table shows the warning sign: patients given drug B were younger (72 v 79 years) and less often had dementia (31% v 46%), so length of stay would differ even if the two drugs were identical. Randomisation is the only reliable answer to confounding by indication. Without it, even thousands of admissions describe who was given each drug, not what the drug did. Some texts call this an observational cohort comparison; either way, allocation was not random.

Rule: Intervention compared without random allocation = quasi-experimental design.
Trap: Assuming that thousands of patients make the comparison fair.

Source: Shadish WR, Cook TD, Campbell DT (2002). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference. Houghton Mifflin.

A PTSD therapy trial uses stratified randomisation by sex, trauma type (single or repeated) and baseline severity (moderate or severe). The table shows the start of each stratum's allocation list. Which statement is FALSE?
  1. A separate random sequence is generated for each stratum
  2. Blocks are usually used within each stratum
  3. Too many strata in a small trial can leave strata nearly empty
  4. The stratification factors end up distributed purely at random between the arms
  5. The factors should be strongly linked to outcome
Show the working
Answer: D The stratification factors end up distributed purely at random between the arms

Working: 2 sexes x 2 trauma types x 2 severity levels = 8 strata. Within each stratum, block randomisation keeps the arms balanced, so the factors are evenly spread by design. Unmeasured factors are still balanced only by chance.

The table shows 8 separate lists, each built from blocks of 4, so options about separate sequences, blocks and the number of strata are all true. Stratification balances the named factors by design, so the false statement is the one claiming they are left to chance.

Rule: Stratification forces balance on chosen factors; it is not left to chance.
Trap: Thinking stratification merely randomises the factors.

What each method balances. Only chance balances what was not measured.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1999). How to randomise. BMJ, 319: 703-704.

Characteristics of the participants already allocated. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In a small multicentre trial of a relapse prevention programme for alcohol dependence, the table shows the participants already allocated. Each new participant goes to whichever arm would best reduce the imbalance in age group, sex and severity, given those already enrolled. What is this method?
  1. Stratified randomisation
  2. Block randomisation
  3. Simple randomisation
  4. Cluster randomisation
  5. Minimisation
Show the working
Answer: E Minimisation

Minimisation balances several factors at once, even in small trials, where stratification would create too many strata. A random element (for example 80% probability of the minimising arm) is usually added to reduce predictability. Central computer allocation keeps it concealed.

With the table: the next participant is aged 40+, female and severe. Matching counts are 6 + 7 + 5 = 18 in arm A and 5 + 6 + 4 = 15 in arm B, so minimisation sends her to arm B. Minimisation looks at those already enrolled and moves the next patient towards balance. It suits small trials with several factors.

Rule: Next allocation depends on those already allocated = minimisation.
Trap: Calling this stratified randomisation.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (2005). Treatment allocation by minimisation. BMJ, 330: 843.

Challenge 30 · 13.3 Experimental studies and trials · 13.3.1.5
During the trialActive (n = 60)Placebo (n = 60)
Extra sleep hygiene sessions per patient (mean)0.42.1
Prescribed a benzodiazepine5 (8%)21 (35%)
Improved at 8 weeks36 (60%)27 (45%)
Care received and outcome by arm. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In a placebo-controlled trial of a new hypnotic, the active tablets taste bitter and the placebo does not, so prescribing psychiatrists can tell who is on placebo. The table shows the care each arm received during the trial. Better blinding of which group would best prevent this bias?
  1. Statisticians
  2. Patients
  3. Ethics committee
  4. Trial sponsors
  5. Treating clinicians
Show the working
Answer: E Treating clinicians

Cointervention bias occurs when one arm receives extra treatment because staff know the allocation. Here, the extra benzodiazepines in the placebo arm would shrink the apparent difference. Blinding prescribers, and recording all concomitant treatments, are the safeguards.

The table shows the extra care: 2.1 v 0.4 extra sleep hygiene sessions per patient and a benzodiazepine for 35% v 8%. That extra treatment narrows the observed difference in improvement to 60% v 45%. Extra care given because the clinician knows the arm is cointervention. Blind the prescribers and record all concomitant treatment.

Rule: Cointervention bias is prevented by blinding the clinicians.
Trap: Blaming patient knowledge.

Source: Schulz KF, Grimes DA (2002). Blinding in randomised trials: hiding who got what. Lancet, 359: 696-700.
